subjects.displayTitle: The divine Physician: diagnosing the needs of an age
subjects.introduction: The All-Knowing Physician, Bahá’u’lláh writes, has His finger on the pulse of mankind; He perceives the disease and prescribes the remedy, and the cure the world needs in one age can never be the same as in another. The image asks us to think of humanity as a single body, stricken by conflict, prejudice and a sickness of conscience that no political nostrum can touch, and to see the Prophets as physicians who first diagnose and only then treat. A wise doctor who once prescribed cooling medicines will order warming ones when the patient’s constitution changes, and the change is the proof of his skill. Holding a medical book, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá observes, is not the same as being healed; someone must know how and when to apply it. When Jesus was criticised for eating with publicans and sinners He answered with the same figure, the physician who goes to the sick [1]. The way ahead passes through the Manifestation as educator and as gardener, the needs of the present day, and the healing of body and spirit together.
subjects.arc: Begin with changing needs and careful diagnosis, examine the healing of humanity as one body, and carry the physician image into compassionate service.

order.why: Open with the pulse of humanity and the needs of an age.
Make diagnosis precede prescription.
shortened: The body politic today is greatly in need of a physician. It is similar to a human body afflicted with severe ailments. A doctor diagnoses the case and prescribes treatment. He does not prescribe, however, until he has made the diagnosis.

order.why: Deepen the knowledge required for effective treatment.
shortened: The Prophets of God, the universal Manifestations, are even as skilled physicians; the world of being is as the body of man; and the divine religions are as the treatment and remedy. The physician must be fully aware and informed of all the parts and organs, the constitution and condition of the patient, in order to prescribe an effective remedy. Indeed, it is from the disease itself that the physician deduces the remedy, for he first diagnoses the ailment and then treats its underlying cause. Until the ailment is properly diagnosed, how can any treatment or remedy be prescribed?

order.why: Join changing remedies to a constant aim of healing.
shortened: The world of man is sick, and that competent Physician knoweth the cure, arising as He doth with teachings, counsels and admonishments that are the remedy for every pain, the healing balm to every wound. It is certain that the wise physician can diagnose his patient's needs at any season, and apply the cure.

The treatment ordered by wise physicians of the past, and by those that follow after, is not one and the same, rather doth it depend on what aileth the patient; and although the remedy may change, the aim is always to bring the patient back to health.

order.why: Read the medical illustration as an explanation of changing religious law.
shortened: The body of the world can be compared to that of a man and the Prophets and Messengers of God to able physicians. A human being does not remain always in the same condition: different ailments occur and each calls for a specific remedy. Thus an able physician does not treat all ailments in the same manner, but varies the treatments and remedies in accordance with the requirements of these various ailments and conditions.
This change and alteration is required by the condition of the patient and is an evident proof of the skill of the physician.

order.why: Name divided humanity as the patient.
Imagine the interdependence of all the body’s members.
shortened: Regard the world as the human body which, though at its creation whole and perfect, hath been afflicted, through various causes, with grave disorders and maladies. Not for one day did it gain ease, nay, its sickness waxed more severe, as it fell under the treatment of ignorant physicians, who gave full rein to their personal desires, and have erred grievously. And if at one time, through the care of an able physician, a member of that body was healed, the rest remained afflicted as before.

order.why: Identify the illnesses of conscience, prejudice and conflict.
shortened: O my beloved one! In this day the world of being is even as a stricken man, and therefore standeth in need of a mighty Physician, that He may diagnose its malady and administer a speedy remedy. This sickness cannot be cured by political nostrums, nor will the treatment of liberty alone suffice to heal it, for the disease pertaineth unto morals and conscience, and hath laid hold upon the very soul and heart of man. We seek, then, such a remedy as shall quicken the soul, educate the conscience, endue hearts with a new life, and train the human race in the perfections of the Merciful.

order.why: Consider unity as the sovereign remedy.
shortened: That which the Lord hath ordained as the sovereign remedy and mightiest  instrument for the healing of all the world is the union of all its peoples in one universal Cause, one common Faith.  This can in no wise be achieved except through the power of a skilled, an all-powerful and inspired Physician.

Each time that Most Mighty Instrument hath come, and that Light shone forth from the Ancient Dayspring, He was withheld by ignorant physicians who, even as clouds, interposed themselves between Him and the world.  It failed, therefore, to recover, and its sickness hath persisted until this day.

order.why: Ask what happens when a remedy is applied without wisdom.
shortened: The purpose of these statements is to make it abundantly clear that the Divine religions, the holy precepts, the heavenly teachings, are the unassailable basis of human happiness, and that the peoples of the world can hope for no real relief or deliverance without this one great remedy. This panacea must, however, be administered by a wise and skilled physician, for in the hands of an incompetent all the cures that the Lord of men has ever created to heal men's ills could produce no health, and would on the contrary only destroy the helpless and burden the hearts of the already afflicted.

order.why: Attend to knowing when a remedy should be used.
shortened: The divine laws and religions are God's dispensary. The remedy for every ailment exists therein. A skilled physician is needed to apply this cure, one who knows when to use these remedies.

order.why: Uses the sick world and the skilled Physician to describe the need for a spiritual remedy.
Distinguish possession of a book from competent application.
shortened: It is possible for a man to hold to a book of medicine and say, "I have no need of a doctor; I will act according to the book; in it every disease is named, all symptoms are explained, the diagnosis of each ailment is completely written out, and a prescription for each malady is furnished; therefore, why do I need a doctor?" This is sheer ignorance. A physician is needed to prescribe. Through his skill the principles of the book are correctly and effectively applied until the patient is restored to health.

order.why: Read the search for hidden causes of illness.
shortened: The Prophets of God are the real Physicians. In whatever age or time They appear They prescribe for human conditions. They know the sicknesses; They discover the hidden sources of disease and indicate the necessary remedy.

order.why: Set prophethood within the continuing need for renewal.
Keep the brief description of the Prophets’ work.
Read the reported diagnosis of a worldwide need.
Consider the report’s contrast between spiritual and political diagnosis.
Keep the particular country and its needs in view.
Read the training attributed to the divine physicians.
shortened: Those physicians studied medicine in the divine school, therefore they diagnosed chronic diseases of human souls and even deadly illnesses of the world and prescribed treatments.

order.why: Connect religious renewal with the seasons.
shortened: There are seasons in the revelation from God, as in the natural year, and just as the Christ manifested the Spirit of God in the flesh and helped the earth in his time, now the message of Baha'Ullah is the medicine of which the world has much need.

order.why: Retain the historically situated account of accommodation and change.
Hear the claim of the One who holds the world’s pulse.
shortened: By God! The Ancient Source hath appeared and in His hand is the pulse of the world. He healeth it as He pleaseth, and verily He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise.

order.why: Attend to the requirement first to ascertain the physician’s skill.
shortened: The physician will doubtless prescribe remedies that are at variance with popular notions, but is it permissible for those who have no knowledge of science and medicine to object? No, by God! On the contrary, they must all acquiesce and follow whatsoever the skilled physician prescribes.
First, the skill of the physician must be ascertained, and once this has been done, he "doeth whatsoever he willeth."

order.why: Read the demanding trust analogy within its historical medical imagery.
Keep the severe surgical image within the text’s account of divine authority.
Consider the difference between seeking a cure and assuming self-sufficiency.
shortened: So listen to what the Physician say, in order to produce consequences of soundness and health. If all the people knew their remedy, there would be no need of the Physician and everybody could treat himself very skillfully.

order.why: Read the danger of preferring unskilled practitioners.
Notice the obstruction of a timely remedy.
shortened: The breath of the divine Messiah was diffused, the All-Knowing Physician appeared from behind the veil, and the skilled and true Healer emerged unconcealed.
Yet ignorant and neglectful physicians devoid of learning have intervened and are preventing the divine and timely remedy from being administered.

order.why: Keep the reported consequences of ineffective treatments.
Consider refusal of the prescribed regimen.
shortened: They are not willing to abide by the advice of the physician, but are trying to break his prescribed regimen. They fly away from him and refuse to touch his medicine.

order.why: Read resistance to care as part of the spiritual problem.
shortened: Glory be to God! What heedlessness and wrath and anger is this, that the patient flees from the physician and nurse, and the wounded one abhors the balm and healing remedy! These are signs of the Lord's wrath. When the patient seeks remedy from the physician, he finds comfort of soul and attains joy of conscience.

order.why: Retain the reported warning concerning persistent neglect.
shortened: They say that the last cure is to burn the malady, as there is no other remedy. This is because the greater the profusion of divine compassion, the deeper are people's neglects; the more protective the grace of God, the more determined is people's rebellion and denial.

order.why: Remember the suffering endured by the healer.
Turn toward divine compassion.
Hear the direct invitation to wounded hearts.
Enter the image of an open hospital.
Turn toward the physician of spirits and hearts.
shortened: Turn your attention to the Most Glorious Beauty, Who is the King of the Kingdom and the Physician of spirits and hearts.

order.why: Connect healing influence with love.
shortened: To-day the penetrative or Executive Power over the spirits, minds and souls is the love of Baha’u’llah, because He is the Promised One of all the nations, the Heavenly Teacher of all the world and the Physician of the hearts and the souls.

order.why: Let the elixir image suggest a remedy reaching the whole.
shortened: The Ancient Physician healeth the nations with a sovereign remedy that penetrateth the nerves and veins - a pure, sufficient and healing elixir.

order.why: Read the urgency of chronic illness.
Consider teachings as remedies and ointments.
Keep the revealed call to listen and receive.
shortened: The Divine Lote-Tree calleth out from the crimson spot, addressing the people of creation, saying: O My chosen ones throughout the lands! Hearken unto My most sweet call and unto My rustling which hath been raised betwixt earth and heaven.

order.why: Read the particular summons to steadfast recognition in its source context.
shortened: Know ye that in this day He hath appeared at the center of the world as the One circumambulating the Most Great Throne, and account all else as non-existent, extinct and forgotten.

order.why: Join recognition with protecting others from heedlessness.
shortened: O Tabib! The True Physician speaketh: Strive ye to protect humankind from the disease of ignorance and heedlessness through the power of the Lord of Destiny, and heal them through this supreme remedy which is the recognition of the Lord of all peoples.

order.why: Introduce the believer as a loving physician.
shortened: The divine friends must, like skilled physicians with sincere intention, become healers of the afflicted and loving physicians to the sick, so that perhaps the breath of life may be inhaled in those regions, a gentle breeze may blow and give life to the lifeless ones and make them fresh and verdant.

order.why: Let bodily weakness coexist with a capacity to help others.
Read the responsibility to attend to wounds of heart and soul.
Apply the principle of diagnosis before treatment to spiritual service.
Distinguish kind truthfulness from hostility.
Consider evidence and understanding as a healing resource.
Notice the attention given to deep wounds.
shortened: O spiritual friend! The skilled physician and expert doctor treats chronic illnesses and cures severe diseases. He applies healing salves to deep wounds and uses superior poultices for crushing blows.

order.why: Read the call to apply the remedy with divine assistance.
shortened: Therefore, with the help and favor of the Ancient Beauty, skilled physicians must treat them with the most great universal remedy.

order.why: Ask for the capacities needed for this service.
Consider the image of purification through spiritual ingredients.
Join the task to prayer for humanity’s health.
Offer gratitude for being guided toward help.
shortened: Praise be unto Thee for Thou hast guided every thirsty one to the Fountain of Life and every ailing one to the Merciful Physician.

order.why: Include oneself among those in need of healing.
shortened: O God! We are all sick and Thou art the Kind Physician! Heal our spiritual diseases! Lead us toward the road of Thy Kingdom! Deliver us from the vices of the world of nature and adorn our beings with the virtues of Thy Kingdom.

order.why: Close with remembrance as a source of restoration.

questions: What changes when the divisions of humanity are understood as ailments of one shared body?
How can different remedies serve the same purpose of healing in different ages or circumstances?
What distinguishes wise application of a teaching from merely possessing or repeating it?
What does Jesus’ physician image add by placing the need for care at the center of his response to criticism?
How can a person offer an honest, helpful word while remaining conscious of their own need for healing?
Which connected image—educator, gardener, or source of light—might deepen your understanding of the work described here?

references.label: 1 · Mark 2:13–17 · The physician and those in need
references.note: After calling Levi and eating with publicans and sinners, Jesus responds to criticism with the image of a physician attending those who are sick. Compare the priority given to need and restoration with the compilation’s images of spiritual and social healing. The passages share a healing image while developing it in different settings: a meal and a call to repentance, and the changing needs of humanity across religious dispensations.

subjects.displayTitle: Bearing fruit: what a life gives to others
subjects.introduction: A tree may tower and stay green all summer and still give no one anything to eat. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá returns to that image again and again, and it carries a gentle severity: the fruit of a human life, he says, is love, and with it truthfulness, trustworthiness, regard for parents, and conduct that makes faith believable to those who watch. Bahá’u’lláh calls His servants the trees of His garden and asks that others may profit from what they bear. Neither a long life nor polished learning settles the matter; some trees ripen early, and their brief season is already complete. Jesus, in Luke, traces good fruit back to the treasure of the heart [1], and here too the outward harvest depends on what grows within. Such fruit is never forced. It needs rain, light and patient tending, gifts that come from beyond the tree itself. The questions it raises lead naturally toward the cultivation of the soul as living soil, toward work offered as worship, and toward the quiet radiance of goodly deeds.
subjects.arc: Begin with love and good character as fruit, connect inner life with work and service, and balance responsibility with cultivation, grace, and humility.

order.why: Give the metaphor an explicit spiritual and ethical meaning.
shortened: A tree must be fruitful; it may be very tall, very verdant, but yielding no fruits. The fruits of the tree of human life are the Love of God, magnetic, spiritual susceptibilities, heavenly illumination, the knowledge of God, praiseworthy attributes, good morals and conducts.

order.why: Open with the simple naming of love as fruit.
shortened: Man is like a tree. The tree lives to produce fruit. The fruit of man is love.

order.why: Name trustworthiness, truthfulness and care for parents.
Widen the fruits toward the healing of nations.
shortened: I hope that each one of you may become a tree laden with delicious fruits for the healing of the nations!

order.why: Ask how conduct affects another person’s trust.
shortened: Consider for example a tree - before its fruits appear, if it is described, some people will acknowledge it while others will waver between acceptance and denial until the fruits appear. And after the fruit appears, if it is bitter, they will surely reject the descriptions of that describer and all will arise in denial, both those who wavered and those who accepted. Thus the tree of human existence becomes known and proven by the fruits of deeds, and all observe its acts and deeds. If they find them good and pleasant they will surely accept, and without this they will surely turn away.

order.why: Test a conception of God through love for other people.
shortened: A. It is as difficult for the human mind to understand the Essence of God as for the watch to understand its maker, but through the Manifestations it becomes easier to understand His Spirit and therefore to draw near it. Otherwise, we must form for ourselves a mental conception of God, which may be a false one. The only test of its truth lies in the influence this conception has upon our lives; if it makes us kind and loving in our relations with our fellow-men, we may know it is a true one. In other words, it must produce in our hearts a love of God, which must be transmuted into love for man.

order.why: Read the reported test of spiritual experience by its fruit.
Connect the claim to spirituality with life-giving deeds.
shortened: That which is truly spiritual must light the path to God, and must result in deeds. We cannot believe the call to be spiritual when there is no result. Spirit is reality, and when the spirit in each of us seeks to join itself with the Great Reality, it must in turn give life.

order.why: Bring fruitfulness into useful work and care for kindred.
shortened: Ye are the trees of My garden; ye must give forth goodly and wondrous fruits, that ye yourselves and others may profit therefrom. Thus it is incumbent on every one to engage in crafts and professions, for therein lies the secret of wealth, O men of understanding! For results depend upon means, and the grace of God shall be all-sufficient unto you. Trees that yield no fruit have been and will ever be for the fire.
The best of men are they that earn a livelihood by their calling and spend upon themselves and upon their kindred for the love of God, the Lord of all worlds.

order.why: Read the criticism of idleness within its stated setting.
shortened: Despite manifest blindness and ignorance they pride themselves on their insight and knowledge. Among them are mystics who bear allegiance to the Faith of Islam, some of whom indulge in that which leadeth to idleness and seclusion. I swear by God! It lowereth man's station and maketh him swell with pride. Man must bring forth fruit. One who yieldeth no fruit is, in the words of the Spirit, like unto a fruitless tree, and a fruitless tree is fit but for the fire.

order.why: Distinguish abundant appearance from an actual harvest.
shortened: What is the sum-total and upshot of farming, ploughing, sowing the seeds and irrigating? Is there any of the thought behind all these labors save the gathering of crops? If the sheaves are only green and verdant but having no grains of wheats or barleys, the result is not achieved. The aim has not been the luxuriant verdancy of the field, but the richness of the harvest. I hope the believers will do their utmost to crown their lives with abundant harvest.

order.why: Keep spiritual fruit distinct from worldly accomplishment.
shortened: The tree, no matter how green or beautiful it may be, if it is not fruitful, it is useless. So you will see many trees which are green and fresh, but produce no fruit. In the same way you see a man in the world who is very wise, learned, refined, accomplished, and diplomatic, but he is deprived of the Bounty of the Kingdom, and will not possess a share of it. But it is possible to see a man who is not accomplished or educated but who still has a share in the Bounty of the Kingdom, and when he attains to the Bounty of the Kingdom, of course he will be a fruitful tree.

order.why: Read the emergence of potential into visible character.
shortened: ...man is like unto a tree, and trees yield diverse fruits. A goodly tree must needs bring forth delectable fruits, that its true nature and essence may emerge from behind the veil of potentiality and become clear and manifest. For this is the age of resurrection and gathering, when the reality of all things becomes evident and apparent.

order.why: Hear the summons to manifest what is hidden.
Introduce the season of fruit and harvest.
Keep the concise call to the present moment.
shortened: Now is the time for the appearance of fruit.

order.why: Read opportunity through the images of trees and lights.
Return attention from past claims to present benefit.
shortened: We have nothing to do with the past. "What has passed is past. And what is to come has not appeared. Therefore do not compare two nothings." If any of them becomes a believer in this Day, then he is considered the essence of the world of humanity. If a tree was fruit-bearing in the past but is now dead, then it is no longer a tree. Today, it must manifest harvests and fruits. In short, there must be benefits in our endeavors, and we must consider each moment precious.

order.why: Consider the urgency of responding to spiritual springtime.
shortened: If a tree fails to become verdant and flourishing in the springtime through the life-giving divine breeze, and yields no blossoms or fruit, in what season will it become verdant and in what time will it yield fruit? Surely it will be forever deprived and eternally hopeless.

order.why: Read the expectation of fruit after the spring’s passing.
Ask what a finite life carries forward.
shortened: "The life of man will at last end in this world. We must all take out of this life some fruit. The tree of one's existence must bear fruit. If a tree has not fruit you must cut it down and burn it. It would be useless for other purposes.

order.why: Keep the stern image as a demand on one’s own life.
shortened: Human souls must bring forth fruit during their sojourn in this evanescent world, for a fruitless tree is but fit for the fire.

order.why: Retain the concise parallel about results.
Read the contrast between sweetness and bitterness.
Distinguish fruit from leaves and blossoms.
Consider the image of a contribution shining into posterity.
shortened: Trees are of two kinds: those that bear fruit and those that are barren. The fruit-bearing tree is transformed into light and shineth forth from the horizon of posterity. The barren one hath ever been and will continue to be fit for the fire.

order.why: Separate a life’s fruit from its length.
shortened: The purpose of life is to get certain results; that is, the life of man must bring forth certain fruitage. It does not depend upon the length of life. As soon as the life is crowned with fruition then it is completed, although that person may have had a short life. There are certain trees which come to fruition very quickly, but there are other trees which attain to fruition very late; the aim is fruit.

order.why: Read consolation through the particular example of Mr. Chase.
shortened: The results in life are the important things. A man may live a hundred years and if his life be not fruitful, it is of no importance. If he lives here a very short time and his life be fruitful, it is equivalent to being here a hundred thousand years. Importance is to be attached to fruitage. Now, praise God, Mr. Chase did yield fruit.

order.why: Join the completed result with faith, certitude and love.
Invite an honest review of the good accomplished.
shortened: When man departs from this mortal life, he must see in a tangible manner the accumulated results of his several scores of life, and observe whether any good is accomplished by him or not.

order.why: Let a life of service become a source of joy.
shortened: But when one reflects, one should see that his life has been spent in matters that have yielded magnificent results, that their lives are like pure seeds that have formed abundant harvests. This is joy, this is delight.

order.why: Imagine days as pages written by conduct.
shortened: Likewise every day of human life has the status of a leaf from the book and is counted as a page from its pages, and every month is a compilation and every year a manifest book. And deeds and manners and words and actions and conditions and character are like designs and drawings and lines and writing.

order.why: Consider deeds through the returning echo.
Ask what trace and treasury a life leaves.
shortened: Therefore strive that in this world and in the world of the Kingdom thou mayst deposit a treasury and leave behind a trace and a result; - so that day unto day thou mayst become more favored in the divine Threshold and be classed as one of the most faithful and sincere servants of His Holiness Baha'u'llah.

order.why: Extend the horizon of sowing beyond immediate results.
Examine the soil in which the seed of a life is planted.
shortened: Look at the people of the world and observe them carefully. You will see that they are like farmers or gardeners, and though life to all these farmers is very dear yet they are planting the seed of life in poor soil or in sterile ground. The seeds sown in sterile ground are absolutely of no value. Those that are sown in poor soil will grow a while, but later they will wither away and be without result.

order.why: Turn toward the patient work of planting and nurturing.
shortened: Plant such a sapling that it may become fruitful, and nurture such a tree that it may yield fresh fruit.

order.why: Read sustained effort through the gardener and traveler.
Receive the tree’s growth as dependent on gifts beyond itself.
shortened: The sun will shine on it, and it will bear fruits and bring forth goodly results.
It is the same as you have stated.

order.why: Approach the fire of recognition as a source of fruitful life.
Connect guidance with following divine counsel.
shortened: Arise and fulfil the admonitions of the Abha Beauty and follow the path of His counsels so that the glancing beams of thy spirit might illumine the world of humanity and thou mayest guide other souls, and may grow to be a fruit-laden tree in the garden of the All Glorious.

order.why: Read this fruit in the source’s setting of awakening and serving others.
shortened: This is the fruit of existence and this is the divine bounty in the world of the seen and unseen.

order.why: Ask what a meaningful encounter changes afterward.
shortened: Fruits must be the results of these visits. Patients go to a hospital. Some leave but slightly improved. Some leave more ill than when they entered. And some leave entirely cured. I hope you will be of those who are entirely cured.

order.why: Keep the short summons to a good harvest.
Offer shade as well as sweet fruit.
shortened: Become fruitful trees, give sweet fruits, and provide shade so that the soul of 'Abdu'l-Baha may be gladdened and the heart of this wronged one may be freed from the bonds of sorrows.

order.why: Read universal bounty as an invitation to contribute.
shortened: This cycle is the cycle of the most great name, its mercy is universal, its grace and bounty inclusive of the near and far ones extend to the servants, the eager thanks of Abdul-Baha and remind them of the counsels and teachings of the one true Lord so that all may yield crop in this Abha garden and at every moment they may produce a luscious fruit and that they may become the cause of verdure and beauty....

order.why: Let the sequence of luminous images widen the aspiration.
Imagine virtues becoming a fragrance for the world.
shortened: O thou who seekest the beauty of the All Glorious!

In this merciful cycle, this most great dispensation, thou must strive to receive a plenteous share of the divine bestowals, perchance thy goodly virtues will, even as the fragrance of musk, perfume the whole world.

order.why: Keep growth beneath the shade of the divine Word.
shortened: And through the aid and protection of the Blessed Beauty, may you become, under the shade of the Divine Word, fruitful saplings and trees bearing spiritual fruits, may you be the signs of guidance and the standards of the Abha Kingdom, may you be pearls in the shell of grace and dawning-places of the lights of guidance.

order.why: Receive the rain of the Covenant.
Read a prayer for an expanding, nourished branch.
Move from spring’s leaves and blossoms toward true fruit.
Hear the encouragement offered to a fresh plant.
Keep the particular hope for a son’s growth.
Read the personal invitation to become adorned with truth.
Receive the brief hope for fresh fruit.
Connects effective teaching with the prior development of spiritual character and deeds.
Retain the parallel personal encouragement.
shortened: I hope thou wilt become a fruitful tree producing sweet fruits.

order.why: Let the prayer widen toward the highest paradise.
Consider the future influence of fruit not yet visible.
Close the linked readings with fruitfulness in every season.
shortened: May you become as fruitful trees producing luscious fruits for all the seasons.

order.why: Distinguish fallible believers from the measure of a revelation’s authority.
End with the responsibility of those who claim to love the Founder.

questions: What would count as nourishing fruit in a relationship, a household, or a community?
How do the passages distinguish spiritual fruitfulness from impressive appearances or measurable achievement?
What does Luke’s connection between the heart and its outward fruit invite you to notice about your speech and conduct?
How might useful work and care for others become expressions of the same inward life?
What kinds of patient cultivation, help, and receptivity are needed before good intentions can bear fruit?
How can you take responsibility for the effects of a believer’s conduct while remembering the distinction between an imperfect follower and the teachings themselves?

references.label: 1 · Luke 6:43–45 · The tree, its fruit, and the heart
references.note: Jesus moves from knowing a tree by its fruit to the good or evil brought forth from the heart, including what a person says. Compare this inward-outward relation with the compilation’s accounts of love, character, and useful action. The image invites attention to the quality and origin of what a life offers, rather than treating visible activity alone as evidence of spiritual growth.

subjects.introduction: A tree grows tall, bears fruit for years, and at last stands barren; then the Husbandman takes its seed and plants it in fresh soil, and the same tree rises again, young. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá returns to this image again and again, because it holds a difficult truth gently: what comes back in a new spring is not the old individual but the old qualities, the colour and fragrance of last year’s rose in this year’s bloom. Religion, He teaches, moves through seasons in just this way, and the storms of winter are themselves the makers of the next spring. Ecclesiastes, with its times for planting and uprooting and its humility before the whole design, offers a kindred wisdom [1]. The question these seasons press on a life is how to discern what the present one requires, and that question opens outward into the spiritual springtime, the return of the Manifestations of God, and the difference between the ephemeral and the eternal.
subjects.arc: Begin with renewal through seed and spring, explore the meaning of return, and read hardship and opportunity through the changing requirements of a season.

order.why: Introduce material and spiritual cycles together.
shortened: In this material world, time has changing cycles and place is subject to varying conditions.  Seasons follow one another and individuals progress, regress, and develop.
The spiritual cycles associated with the Prophets of God proceed in like manner. That is, the day of the advent of the Holy Manifestations is the spiritual springtime.
The spiritual cycles of the Sun of Truth, like the cycles of the physical sun, are in a state of perpetual motion and renewal.

order.why: Open with a new tree growing from the old tree’s seed.
Distinguish returning qualities from identical substance.
Develop the seed-to-seed illustration.
Follow the seed through its changing forms.
Keep recurrence of species distinct from reincarnation.
shortened: With respect to the species, however, return and recurrence are plainly visible in material realities; that is, the trees which in years past bore leaves, blossoms and fruits will in the years to come bear the same leaves, blossoms and fruits. This is called recurrence of species.

order.why: Read the renewal of a tree that once sheltered peoples.
Connect the new sapling with renewed revelation.
shortened: Then a new tree grows from its seeds, green, verdant and freshened by the divine outpouring, the merciful breeze, the heat from the Sun of Reality, the heavy rain from the clouds of the abundant mercy and the blowing wind from the wafting place of Providence.  "Whatever verse we abolish or forget we replace by a better one."  This is the example of the new creation, the miraculous cycle and the second resurrection, which is in conformity with the first creation.

order.why: Read the Manifestations’ appearance as springtime.
Keep the concise seasonal correspondence.
Move through the four seasons of the analogy.
Uses the cycle of the sun and seasons to explain spiritual renewal.
Notice the ripening of fruit as well as the opening of spring.
shortened: Now consider the pervasive influence of the sun upon all earthly beings, and behold what visible effects and outcomes result from its proximity or remoteness, its rising or setting. At one time it is autumn, at another it is spring. At one time it is summer, at another it is winter. When the sun crosses the equinox, the life-giving spring appears in all its splendour, and when it reaches the summer solstice, the fruits attain their full maturity, grains and plants yield their produce, and earthly things attain the plenitude of their growth and development.

order.why: Read the distinction between spring’s promise and summer’s harvest.
Explore the larger account of universal cycles in its historical terms.
shortened: In the same way, the entire universe, whether with respect to the realm of nature or the realm of man, proceeds through cycles of major events and occurrences.

When a cycle comes to a close a new one is inaugurated, and the previous cycle, on account of the momentous events which transpire, vanishes so entirely from memory as to leave behind no record or trace.

Each of the Manifestations of God has likewise a cycle wherein His religion and His law are in full force and effect. When His cycle is ended through the advent of a new Manifestation, a new cycle begins. Thus, cycles are inaugurated, concluded, and renewed, until a universal cycle is completed in the world of existence and momentous events transpire which efface every record and trace of the past; then a new universal cycle begins in the world, for the realm of existence has no beginning.

order.why: Keep the reported account of previous cycles and spiritual purpose.
Read the interval between Manifestations.
shortened: Although the signs of the Most Great Resurrection and the Supreme Catastrophe were specific to the Day of the Manifestation of the Revealer of Sinai, yet His ordinances continue and His outpouring descends and His light shines forth and His dawn gleams bright. For every age has its Day and every cycle is the extended period between two Manifestations.

order.why: Consider dawning, setting, presence and separation.
Retain the concise image of repeated sunrise.
Let the succession of dispensations take the form of prayer.
Distinguish perishing achievements from continuing divine purpose.
shortened: In this mortal world every important matter hath an end; and every remarkable achievement a termination; none having permanent existence. For instance, consider how the important achievements of the ancient world have been totally exterminated and not a trace remaineth therefrom save the great Cause of the Kingdom of God, which hath no beginning and will have no end. At most, it is only renewed.

order.why: Keep the continuing outpouring beside created change.
Distinguish the soul’s progress from material decline.
shortened: All material things progress to a certain point, then begin to decline. This is the law which governs the whole physical creation.

All creation, whether of the mineral, vegetable or animal kingdom, is compelled to obey the law of motion; it must either ascend or descend. But with the human soul, there is no decline. Its only movement is towards perfection; growth and progress alone constitute the motion of the soul.

order.why: Examine motion as a feature of created existence.
shortened: Know that nothing that exists remains in a state of repose--that is, all things are in motion. They are either growing or declining, either coming from non-existence into existence or passing from existence into non-existence. So this flower, this hyacinth, was for a time coming from non-existence into existence and is now passing from existence into non-existence. This is called essential or natural motion, and it can in no wise be dissociated from created things, for it is one of their essential requirements, just as it is an essential requirement of fire to burn.

order.why: Read culmination as the beginning of another condition.
shortened: According to an intrinsic law all phenomena of being attain to a summit and degree of consummation, after which a new order and condition is established.

order.why: Consider the tree’s growth and decay in the reported analogy.
Extend the pattern to lives and dynasties.
Listen to the world’s testimony to transience.
shortened: The world is a manifest book which, at every moment, has borne and continues to bear witness to its own transience. Indeed, from the beginning of the world until now it has proclaimed "Depart! Depart!" and with most eloquent utterance declares: "O servants! Observe the changes in me. At times I appear in the darkness of night, and at other times in the light of dawn. My trees are sometimes seen in the fullness of greenness and freshness, and sometimes appear yellow, withered and dry.

order.why: Read the transformation of bodily elements after death.
Keep the historical account of material journeys distinct from a returning soul.
Consider the reported arcs of emanation and return.
shortened: The Bab and Baha'u'llah  taught: The creation, the emanated, is the descending curve of the Logos (the breath of life of God) and the development (evolution) is the ascending curve; this (curve) is, however, nothing else than the coming back or returning of all things to God, be it for destruction or for absolute perfection.

order.why: Read rotation and renewal in the source’s historical cosmology.
shortened: When anything has been renewed in this contingent world it is found to be in a better condition, and if renewal did not take place from time to time, annihilation would be the result of all contingent beings. If the planets had no rotation they would soon cease to exist. This is the reason that God has ordained rotation and renewal. Even the sun itself revolves around another center.

order.why: Join interdependence with the explicit caution about astrology.
Keep the reported observation of continual change among peoples.
Read the report’s claim concerning recurrent patterns.
Turn to the scriptural language of differing times.
Ask what a season’s requirements mean for response.
shortened: The seasons have their wisdom and the times their requirements.

In springtime the birds of the meadow break into song and the spring season reveals wondrous artistry. The nightingale in this wondrous season grants the listeners their share of various melodies. The dove of the garden of inner meanings is stirred into motion. But in autumn all songs grow silent and the birds of the meadow, placing their heads under the wing of pain and tribulation, cease their songs and melodies.

order.why: Consider the appropriateness of shelter and outward activity.
shortened: In the time of spring the blossoming of the wilderness gives loving pleasure.
But, in the season of falling leaves, it is well to seek shelter and rest within a house. In the time of winter a small room in the simplest dwelling is desired.

order.why: Connect changing conditions with the needs of humanity.
Challenge the thought that one spring suffices forever.
Remember that cultivation can be lost through neglect.
Read the reported account of moral decline.
shortened: However, after the passage of time, once more man returns to his base nature and is seized in the grasp of darkness and unfaithfulness. The original condition is reinstated, the bright day is darkened, the world of humanity becomes the animal world, splendor is transmuted to obscurity, and heavenly attraction turns into fullfilment of carnal desires.

order.why: Move from dormancy toward renewed spiritual life.
shortened: When the divine spring is over and the heavenly bounty ceases, the trees of being lie dormant. Lifelessness and stillness prevail over the world of man.

Then the spiritual spring spreads its tent once more. The gardens of the hearts regain their freshness, charm and verdure. The buds of knowledge open and the anemones of reality appear. The world of man becomes another world,
This is the divine law and is a requirement of the world of creation. This is the cause of the appearance of the many Manifestations of God.

order.why: Hear the announcement of guidance returning.
Keep the recurrence of opposition beside the recurrence of revelation.
shortened: Absolute Being cries out in utter nothingness, saying: At two times is the clamor and cry of the people of contingent existence raised up - once at the beginning, that is, at the first creation, and again at the return. Observe how when the Sun of Truth dawned from the horizon of the Divine Command in the name of Muhammad (may the spirit of all else be sacrificed for His sake), the people of the world rose up in opposition and raised their cry.

order.why: Introduce the storm as an image of preparation.
shortened: If the rain does not pour down, the wind does not blow, the storm and tempest do not rage, - the soul-refreshing spring does not appear. If the clouds do not weep, the meadows do not laugh. The hurricane, and tornado, the cyclone and the blast are the harbingers of the spring.

order.why: Read the argument that all seasons contribute to the whole.
shortened: Yet when you look to reality, all seasons serve the world of existence; without them it would be incomplete. It is winter's revolution, winter's storm, winter's cold, its ice and blizzard that creates the life-giving spring. Without winter's storm, the world of existence would not don new garments in spring. The gentleness of spring comes from winter's severity.

order.why: Develop the winter-to-spring relationship.
Retain the parallel formulation in its own source.
shortened: Until the winter season comes, and lightning strikes, and thunder peals, and snow and rain fall, and ice and storm occur, and the intensity of cold exerts its influence, the life-giving spring does not arrive, and the perfumed breeze does not blow, and moderate weather does not come, and flowers and fragrant herbs do not sprout, and the earth's surface does not become supreme paradise, and trees do not blossom and bring forth leaves and fruit. That intensity of cold and snow and storm and tempest were prerequisites for the appearance of these flowers and fragrant herbs and blossoms and flowers and fruits.

order.why: Consider freshness emerging after harshness.
shortened: But for winter's harsh storms, its rain and snow, and rising waters, the meadow could not smile, its flower patches could not be renewed, the trees could not blossom, the breezes of spring could not bestow their reviving breath, and the musk-laden fragrances could not delight the sense of smell. The gifts, delights, and freshness of the season of spring are the result of the severity and harshness of winter's storms.

order.why: Hear encouragement addressed to friends in difficulty.
Read the capacity to hope beyond a present winter.
shortened: For example, the requirement of winter is cold weather, snow, storm, hail, rain etc. we cannot call a winter a winter unless these things are made possible.

Man alone knows that after every hard winter, the spring with its thousand vari-colored flowers will bloom forth After the velocity of the gale the soul-refreshing breeze will waft. After the sterility and apparent death; fertility and life will manifest. After the hurricane and storm quietness and calmness will reign. After the silence of the birds they will all break forth into joyous songs of spring.

order.why: Join steadfastness with awareness of alternating conditions.
shortened: May you bear these trials and tests most willingly and joyously, for every night is followed by a day, and every day has a night.
Every spring has an autumn, and every autumn has its spring.

order.why: Approach the seasons through gratitude and divine names.
Let the language of renewed life become vivid.
Follow the movement from bare earth to a laughing meadow.
Read the blossoming of knowledge and meaning.
shortened: The spiritual spring hath appeared, and the April clouds, through divine bounty, have bestowed pearls and gems. The rain clouds of the Lord's mercy, through the outpourings of mysterious grace, have made the garden's expanse a supreme paradise and adorned the spiritual gardens with the anemones of truth and meaning. From every direction the flowers of the meadow have shown their faces and appeared in the utmost freshness and grace, and the birds of dawn have been stirred and have sung and spoken the mysteries of love.

order.why: Keep the personal welcome of springtime.
Consider the emergence of capacities previously concealed.
Close with the continuing process of spiritual resurrection.

questions: What can remain continuous when the outward forms of a life or a religious community change?
How does the distinction between returning qualities and an identical returning individual shape your reading of the seed and flower images?
What does the soul’s continuing progress add to a collection otherwise rich in images of growth and decline?
How does Ecclesiastes complicate or enrich the hope of renewal expressed here?
How can the winter imagery encourage endurance without making us passive toward suffering that can be relieved?
What might it mean to discern the needs of the present season in your own life or in a community’s development?

references.label: 1 · Ecclesiastes 3:1–11 · A time for each purpose
references.note: The passage places planting and uprooting, mourning and dancing, silence and speech within an account of differing times. It then acknowledges the limits of human knowledge of God’s work as a whole. Compare that combination of change and humility with the compilation’s seasonal images. Ecclesiastes does not itself set out the Bahá’í account of successive Manifestations; the comparison asks how timing affects understanding and action.

subjects.introduction: Bahá’u’lláh ordained a payment and then forbade anyone to ask for it. That double gesture is the whole character of Ḥuqúqu’lláh, the Right of God: nineteen parts in a hundred of what one acquires beyond a set threshold belong to God, the duty is binding, and yet the offering is acceptable only when it comes spontaneously, with joy and radiance, from a person reminded but never pressed. Demanding it is not permitted; an offering that diminished the dignity of the Cause by a mustard seed would be refused though it were the wealth of the world. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá roots the institution in the readiness of people who belong to one another to give even their lives for each other, and Bahá’u’lláh says its purpose is to purify what we possess and to draw us near. Paul’s counsel that God loves a cheerful giver, and that such giving supplies the needs of others and overflows in thanksgiving, offers a kindred account of intention [1]. The historical letters that trace the law’s early years differ in figures and in particular instructions, so the official explanation of the rate, the exemptions and the role of conscience is the steady reference point [2]. The journey continues into the interconnectedness of all things and into the laws of the Kitáb-i-Aqdas, where freedom and obligation are meant to grow together.
subjects.arc: Begin with mutual assistance and willing generosity, examine the obligation and its qualifications, and follow the historical record of trust, administration, and charitable use.

order.why: Place willingness and joy at the center.
Open with cooperation as the institution’s foundation.
shortened: Now consider, if among the people who are merely the manifestations of the world of being this significant matter is of such importance, how much greater must be the spirit of co-operation and mutual assistance among those who are the essences of the world of creation, who have sought the sheltering shadow of the heavenly Tree, and are favoured by the manifestations of divine grace; and how the evidences of this spirit should, through their earnest endeavour, their fellowship and concord, become manifest in every sphere of their inner and outer lives, in the realm of the spirit and divine mysteries and in all things related to this world and the next. Thus there can be no doubt that they must be willing even to offer up their lives for each other.
This is the basic principle on which the institution of Huququ'llah is established, inasmuch as its proceeds are dedicated to the furtherance of these ends.

order.why: Keep dignity above the size of an offering.
shortened: Action must occur with willingness. In all matters the exaltation of the Cause of God must be observed. We wrote before that if someone owned the whole world and were to give it all but diminish the dignity of the Cause by even a mustard seed, forsaking that wealth would be necessary and obligatory.

order.why: Distinguish obligation from demanding payment.
shortened: Regarding what thou didst write about the Huququ'llah, the firm divine ordinance hath been revealed in the Book, and this matter dependeth upon the acceptance of the souls themselves, for God, exalted be His glory, looking to His previous mercy, hath informed all of what hath been prescribed in the Book. Blessed are they that act! Demanding it is not and hath never been beloved.

order.why: Read the benefit as returning to the giver.
Consider words that attract hearts without pressure.
Keep the explicit prohibition on insistence.
Read the condition governing acceptance.
Distinguish general reminders from demands.
Turn to the central revealed provisions.
shortened: Should anyone acquire one hundred mithqals of gold, nineteen mithqals thereof are God's and to be rendered unto Him, the Fashioner of earth and heaven. Take heed, O people, lest ye deprive yourselves of so great a bounty. This We have commanded you, though We are well able to dispense with you and with all who are in the heavens and on earth; in it there are benefits and wisdoms beyond the ken of anyone but God, the Omniscient, the All-Informed. Say: By this means He hath desired to purify what ye possess and to enable you to draw nigh unto such stations as none can comprehend save those whom God hath willed.

order.why: Connect the obligation with purification and blessing.
Consider the promised benefit for the giver and posterity.
Approach the act through gratitude.
shortened: Thank thou and bless thou the Lord for He hath allowed thee to offer Him the Right of God. This is verily a special favor on His part, for thee; praise Him then for this commandment that is set forth in the Scriptures of thy Lord, of Him that is the Ancient of Days.

order.why: Read the qualities associated with fulfilling the law.
shortened: Huquq has been made obligatory and binding in the Book of God, as it is the cause of progress, steadfastness, firmness and the attainment of blessings for the giver.

order.why: Keep the concise praise of those who act.
shortened: Today the payment of Huququ'llah is a most momentous deed. A hundred thousand blessings upon those souls who have held fast to the Book of God and acted according to it.

order.why: Notice the qualification concerning possibility.
Introduce the threshold and deduction of expenses.
Distinguish the threshold from the rate and trace delayed collection.
shortened: The basic threshold upon which Huquq becomes applicable is nineteen, and this accords with the Most Holy Book, for in that verse the intention was to explain the amount, not the threshold.
Although the Most Holy Book was revealed from the heaven of the Cause several years ago and the law of Huquq was established therein, nevertheless until this year They did not command its collection.

order.why: Read the worked example of nineteen percent.
Consider expenses, livelihood and a payment already made.
Keep tools of livelihood among the qualifications.
Read the specific ruling concerning shop equipment.
Consider the case of nonproductive property and threatened livelihood.
Retain the instruction concerning annual excess and property sales.
Keep the personal prohibition on selling property for payment.
shortened: Regarding the properties you wrote about selling to pay the Huquq - this is absolutely not permitted. As for the Huquq that has become due from you, I beseech with utmost supplication at the Divine Threshold that it be forgiven. Therefore, do not touch the properties at all.

order.why: Explains the minimum amount and the principle that Huququ’llah is paid once on the same property.

sourceQuestion.text: 8. QUESTION:  Concerning the basic sum on which Huququ'llah is payable.

order.why: Distinguish later increases from sums already assessed.
Read the reported explanation that agrees with the stated rate.
Retain the differing reported fraction with the official clarification in view.
Preserve the historical report without adopting its numerical discrepancy or stereotype.
shortened: Q. --What is the Command regarding the giving of tithes: Is it 19% of the increase of one's capital, or it is the one-nineteenth part of one's income?

A. --It should be the one-nineteenth part of one's income. This tithe giving is a blessed privilege. Among mankind money is the greatest thing. This giving will confirm the people. With this money many great works will be done. In Hamadan in Persia, the Jewish believers raised much money in this way. At first I did not accept this money, but later on I directed that it should be used in their own town for the Baha'i school. This giving was a great spiritual blessing to those believers.

order.why: Keep the additional reported fractions distinct from the clarified law.
Read the Bábí provision in its own dispensation.
Locate the account of khums in its religious setting.
Return to the prescription recorded in the Tablets.
Trace permission to receive payments after an earlier delay.
Read the appointment of trustees and the suspended collection.
shortened: For several years the matter of Huquq was suspended, as permission for its collection had not been issued from the Source of the Cause. In recent years this blessed word shone forth from the tongue of the Divine Unity - exalted be His utterance: "Whosoever desires to pay the Huququ'llah, let the Trustees receive it." The Trustees have been mentioned in the Book of God, and this decree was revealed and sent down from the heaven of the Cause purely as a bounty, in consideration of certain benefits, and its advantage returns to the servants themselves.

order.why: Keep the history of acceptance beside the prohibition on solicitation.
shortened: However, in recent years We have, in view of the exigencies of the times, accepted the payment of the Huquq, but have forbidden solicitation thereof. Everyone must have the utmost regard for the dignity of the Word of God and for the exaltation of His Cause. Were a person to offer all the treasures of the earth at the cost of debasing the honour of the Cause of God, were it even less than a grain of mustard, such an offering would not be permissible. All the world hath belonged and will always belong to God. If one spontaneously offereth Huquq with the utmost joy and radiance it will be acceptable, and not otherwise. The benefit of such deeds reverteth unto the individuals themselves.

order.why: Consider the particular circumstances described in this correspondence.
shortened: Until this year, this servant always heard these words from the tongue of Grandeur regarding the Huququ'llah, saying that no one should demand Huququ'llah from anyone, as this depends on the success and pleasure of the servants themselves to pay with complete contentment and submission. However, this year, in view of current affairs and apparent conditions, He said that each of the loved ones of God upon whom Huququ'llah has become binding must pay it. We beseech God that all may be enabled to do this, as this matter is truly the cause of preservation and purity of wealth and of blessing, and has ever been so.

order.why: Read the named routes for transmitting payments.
Attend to the requirement for trustworthy recipients.
Notice the practical provision for a receipt.
shortened: And whosoever desires with utmost longing to pay the Huququ'llah should give it to such trusted ones as yourself and obtain a receipt, so that whatever transpires may occur with the permission and leave of the Truth.

order.why: Read the appointment of a trustee.
Keep the particular delegation of responsibilities.
shortened: Therefore, in compliance with the precept of reward which is ordained by the Lord of Utterance, thou hast been appointed as Trustee of the Huquq and should presently, through the strengthening grace and bounty of the All-Merciful, take up this duty in Tihran, inasmuch as Jinab-i-Amin will occasionally travel to the outlying provinces.

order.why: Retain the short response concerning further instructions.
Receive acknowledgement of contributions from women and men.
Read the acknowledgement within the letter’s circumstances.
shortened: We beseech God to assist those who have acted according to what they were commanded in the Book and to send down upon them from the heaven of His grace a blessing and mercy and benediction from His presence. Verily He is the Mighty, the Bestower. In truth the matter of divine rights is a great matter, incumbent upon all to fulfill, for it is the cause of bounty and blessing and goodness and whatsoever accompanies every soul in every world of the worlds of their Lord, the Self-Sufficient, the Generous.

order.why: Keep the correction concerning whose name a payment bore.
shortened: O beloved of my heart! Ustad 'Ali-Akbar-i-Banna, upon him be the Glory of God, has written from the people of Ya to Hadrat-i-Ism-i-Jud, upon him be the Most Glorious Glory of God. My brother Ustad Kazim, from whom no good effects have been witnessed, has multiple veils. Among them is that this humble one had sent two payments for the Huquq - once through Jinab-i-Amin, upon him be the Glory of God, and once through His Honor Afnan, upon him be all the Most Glorious Glory. One payment arrived and they wrote it in my brother Ustad Kazim's name.

order.why: Follow the particular transfer through named intermediaries.
Read the allocation to a trustee for action under instruction.
Retain the particular sum previously promised.
Keep the detailed historical distribution intact.
Read the instruction to allocate part locally.
Hear the needs of distressed people in the particular distribution.
See education and care of orphans among the uses described.
Connect giving with care for poor and vulnerable people.
Read the particular building proposal.
Keep the urgent construction expense in its historical context.
shortened: It is the exaltation of the Word of God and the manifestation of the greatness of the Cause that after fifty years, the revered House has once again been raised up despite the enemies, and it must be built in utmost glory. Since 'Abdu'l-Baha absolutely does not wish to impose on anyone, you and Jenab-i-Amin must send with utmost speed ten thousand tumans from what is available to Haji Mahmud Qassabchi in Baghdad, for the construction of the House requires at least thirty or forty thousand tumans, and this is among the most pressing expenses that cannot be delayed. According to the people, it is more obligatory than prayer.

order.why: Read permission to spend as a particular instruction, not a general rule.
Acknowledge the material hardship described.
Retain the particular situation of service and wayfaring.
shortened: That which you wrote concerning the mention and service of the friends of God, especially regarding the honored friend J.L.H., may the glory and favors of God rest upon him, and his intention, as well as the payment of the Huququ'llah by all, was presented at the Most Holy Court. His blessed and exalted Word: "Praise be to God, they are blessed with His favors, steadfast in service, speaking His praise and turned toward His face. However, since they are engaged in service and their station is that of the friends and wayfarers, the payment of the Huquq depends on their own will.

order.why: Close with the supplied account of spiritual formation and charitable purpose.

questions: How might the connection between giving and mutual assistance change the way possessions are understood?
What does it mean for an obligation to be left to conscience and fulfilled with joy?
How can education about a spiritual duty preserve freedom from pressure?
What does Paul’s account of cheerful giving illuminate about intention, sufficiency, and the needs of others?
What does the historical correspondence reveal about the importance of trust, clear records, and attention to particular circumstances?
How might the connected subjects of interdependence and divine law deepen a discussion of personal responsibility and collective well-being?

references.label: 1 · 2 Corinthians 9:6–12 · Cheerful giving and shared need
references.note: Paul joins willing, cheerful giving with good works, the supply of others’ needs, and thanksgiving to God. Compare the relation between intention and communal benefit with the repeated insistence on joy in this compilation. The parallel concerns the spiritual character of giving; it does not make the two traditions’ financial provisions identical.

references.label: 2 · The Kitáb-i-Aqdas, note 125 · Rate, exemptions, and conscience
references.note: The official note explains the nineteen-percent rate, the threshold, assessment of subsequent increases, and exemptions including the residence. It also states that fulfilment is left to each Bahá’í’s conscience and that individuals may not be approached to pay. Its references lead to the relevant Questions and Answers. Consult this clarification when reading numerical discrepancies in historical reports and particular administrative instructions retained here.

subjects.displayTitle: The limits of reason: learning with humility
subjects.introduction: The mind, Bahá’u’lláh says, is the greatest sign in a human being, and in the same breath He observes that it cannot see the palm tree in the date-stone until the eye has first seen a palm. That pairing of praise and limit runs through everything the Writings teach about the intellect. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá points to the philosophers who all relied on reason and all disagreed, as proof that reason is a magnificent instrument but not an infallible measure of everything. The eye is dazzled by the sun; the sea does not fit in a cup; a creature with no sense of sight cannot reach colour by hearing harder. Learning can even become a veil, nourishing a pride that shuts its owner out from the very thing all knowledge exists to find, unless it is joined to love, when every science becomes a blessed tree. Socrates’ discovery that those who knew a craft imagined they knew everything is a companion in this humility [1]. The path continues into rational arguments and the mind’s power of discovery, into the four ways of acquiring knowledge.
subjects.arc: Begin with the mind’s dignity and fallibility, explore the limits of perception and conceptual claims, and return to learning enriched by character and humility.

order.why: Distinguish progressive investigation from an infallible criterion.
shortened: This human world is an ocean of varying opinions. If reason is the perfect standard and criterion of knowledge, why are opinions at variance and why do philosophers disagree so completely with each other? This is a clear proof that human reason is not to be relied upon as an infallible criterion. For instance, great discoveries and announcements of former centuries are continually upset and discarded by the wise men of today.

order.why: Open with the mind’s exalted station and acknowledged limits.
shortened: Verily the mind is the greatest sign in man, and blessed is he who attaineth unto it. Yet notwithstanding its lofty station and exalted rank, it is seen to be powerless to comprehend most things, for the mind's knowledge dependeth upon the testimony of sight. Unless the eye beholdeth the palm tree, the mind cannot perceive in the date-stone its fruits and leaves, branches and boughs.

order.why: Read the intellect’s role in understanding what the eye sees.
shortened: Nevertheless, though it is the function of this light to make things visible to us, it cannot give us the power to see them or to understand what their various charms may be, for this light has no intelligence, no consciousness. It is the light of the intellect which gives us knowledge and understanding, and without this light the physical eyes would be useless.

order.why: Explains how the limitations of understanding can affect the perception of religious truth.
Examine philosophers’ changing conclusions.
shortened: The second criterion is that of the intellect, which was the principal criterion of comprehension for those pillars of wisdom, the ancient philosophers. They deduced things through the power of the mind and relied on rational arguments: all their arguments are based upon reason. But despite this, they diverged greatly in their opinions. They would even change their own views: for twenty years they would deduce the existence of something through rational arguments, and then afterwards they would disprove the same, again through rational arguments.

order.why: Place the errors of sense and reason together.
Read concrete examples of perceptual error.
shortened: The senses mistake a mirage for water; the eyes see the sun move; your train or boat seems immobile and the landscape seems to pass by, planets look like fixed points of light; but they have measurable dimensions. A lighted point set in rotation appears like a circle. These examples show the senses subject to error. How can we put our trust in them?

The test of logic is just as imperfect, for were this criterion perfect there would never have been the continual clash of opinion as to the sacred texts. How can they be interpreted by logic if the means be at fault?

order.why: Consider disagreement as a challenge to claims of final certainty.
shortened: Though by the ancient philosophers the reasoning mind was regarded as the highest authority, these philosophers do not agree. Some declare that the universe had a beginning, others that it had no beginning. Their various opinions are so numerous that one cannot count them. But if the verdict of man's reason was a norm of final and absolute verity, the philosophers of the world would agree.

order.why: Keep the reported argument about absolute accuracy.
Retain the parallel account in its own terms.
shortened: While they were thinking this to be the only way one could understand everything they became of different opinions. Discord and differences only show the measure of the intellect to be untrue, for they all had the same intellect, and were this the true standard they would never have disagreed.

order.why: Examine the role of observation in the seed analogy.
shortened: The perception of the mind is bound to the testimony of sight. Before observation, knowledge of all things is concealed from the intellect. Can the rational soul, ere it hath witnessed, behold within the seed the world of trees and fruits, of leaves and branches and twigs? No, by God! When through sight these matters are discovered, the mind then becomes aware of their individual comprehension. Likewise, observe and ponder upon other things.

order.why: Read the reported distinction among kinds of light.
Distinguish instinctive sensitivity from intellectual understanding.
Keep the humorous report in its historical setting.
Read the critique of reducing knowledge to sensation.
Retain the related reported comparison.
Ask whether a limit of perception disproves what exceeds it.
Keep ignorance distinct from a proof of nonexistence.
Let the worm’s confined world make the question vivid.
Read the image of investigation from within a cage.
Consider the analogy’s application to the future life.
shortened: Now these degrees all belong to one kingdom, are all composed of matter. As it is impossible for these different kingdoms belonging to the same world to understand one another to is it impossible for man to understand the things of the future life. For as the difference between these grades or conditions so is the difference between man and the spiritual kingdom. It is impossible for man to perceive or understand it because he has no power with which to perceive it.

order.why: Ask what faculties spiritual perception would require.
Contemplate the cup before the sea and the eye before the sun.
Read the limits of encompassing the divine through prayer.
shortened: O Lord! The innermost reality of understanding in this contingent realm is, in its essence, utterly powerless to grasp even a single one of the mysteries of the All-Merciful, inasmuch as all understanding encompasseth that reality in the realm of existence that is comprehensible. How, then, could that which is contingent comprehend the Ancient Mystery unless the Ancient be encompassed by the contingent world?

order.why: Distinguish a mental conception from the reality it claims to contain.
shortened: For contingent beings are limited by their inability to know Him - otherwise, through the intensification of the bonds of waywardness, the heedless ones would claim knowledge of the essence of the All-Merciful. Yet all that they distinguish through vain imaginings, in the most precise meanings of expression, is but a mental conception or a heart's fancy that can neither quench the thirsty one nor heal the afflicted.

order.why: Keep the concise admission of incomprehensibility.
shortened: To man, the Essence of God is incomprehensible, so also are the worlds beyond this, and their condition.

order.why: Read the Báb’s formulation of limited perception.
shortened: Since minds can only perceive things as limited, they cannot witness the matter between matters and the decree of eternity in the decree of determination.

order.why: Keep the particular critique of philosophical solutions in context.
Let understanding confess its limits in devotional language.
shortened: My God! The wings of our understanding have grown weary of ascending to the zenith of Thy knowledge, and the spiders of our minds are powerless to weave with their threads upon the highest horizons the loftiness of Thy praise and glorification.

order.why: Read humility as a condition of mystical knowledge.
Question claims about realms not yet understood.
Notice the use of sensible language for abstract realities.
Consider the inner veils of imitation and fancy.
Examine how learning can nourish pride.
shortened: Amongst the people is he whose learning hath made him proud, and who hath been debarred thereby from recognizing My Name, the Self-Subsisting; who, when he heareth the tread of sandals following behind him, waxeth greater in his own esteem than Nimrod.

We have decreed, O people, that the highest and last end of all learning be the recognition of Him Who is the Object of all knowledge; and yet, behold how ye have allowed your learning to shut you out, as by a veil, from Him Who is the Dayspring of this Light, through Whom every hidden thing hath been revealed.

order.why: Return knowledge to its intended direction.
shortened: Say: O concourse of divines! We have ordained knowledge that it might guide you to My path, yet ye turned away therefrom and waxed proud before the All-Wise One.

order.why: Read the Báb’s account of learning in relation to the divine Word.
Hear the suffering expressed through the language of formal learning.
shortened: O questioner! Know that people take pride in knowledge and praise it, yet this servant complains of it. Were it not for knowledge, the Beauty would not have been imprisoned in the Most Great Prison of Akka, nor would He have drunk the cup of tribulation at the hands of His enemies. Rhetoric has distanced me, the science of meanings has brought me low, mention of union has disjointed my limbs, brevity has become the cause of prolixity in my hardship and tribulation, morphology has turned me from rest, syntax has erased joy and delight from my heart, and my knowledge of God's mysteries has become chains around my neck.

order.why: Read the warning about attributing personal constructions to religion.
shortened: Leave aside the books of the people - a command from Us - and take hold of this Mighty Tablet. They have authored them according to their desires and attributed them to the religion of God and His path.

order.why: Keep the critique of fruitless interpretations in its communal setting.
Read the reported contrast between contradictory theories and reality.
Consider simplicity as a passage through conflicting accounts.
Retain the fragmentary source with its review notice.
Notice access to grace beyond prestigious learning.
shortened: This grace is all-encompassing and unlimited, such that some handmaidens have attained this station while most of the learned ones of the age, despite their great knowledge, remain deprived and excluded.

order.why: Read truth as available to the pure in heart.
Consider the reported distinction between gathered water and rainfall.
Keep the Báb’s account of innate utterance.
shortened: There is no doubt that I have not been, nor am I, versed in the formal disciplines of the doctors; rather, from the tongue of innate nature there issued supplications and verses which, in very truth, conform to the wonted practice of the People of God -- upon them be God's peace.

order.why: Join moral education with learning as light upon light.
shortened: Training in morals and good conduct is far more important than book learning. A child that is cleanly, agreeable, of good character, well-behaved -- even though he be ignorant -- is preferable to a child that is rude, unwashed, ill-natured, and yet becoming deeply versed in all the sciences and arts. The reason for this is that the child who conducts himself well, even though he be ignorant, is of benefit to others, while an ill-natured, ill-behaved child is corrupted and harmful to others, even though he be learned. If, however, the child be trained to be both learned and good, the result is light upon light.

order.why: Test the tree of knowledge by its fruit in love.
shortened: And every branch of learning, conjoined with the love of God, is approved and worthy of praise; but bereft of His love, learning is barren -- indeed, it bringeth on madness. Every kind of knowledge, every science, is as a tree: if the fruit of it be the love of God, then is it a blessed tree, but if not, that tree is but dried-up wood, and shall only feed the fire.

order.why: Keep good deeds praiseworthy while considering their motives.
shortened: Briefly, good deeds become perfect and complete only after the knowledge of God has been acquired, the love of God has been manifested, and spiritual attractions and goodly motives have been attained.  Otherwise, though good deeds be praiseworthy, if they do not spring from the knowledge of God, from the love of God, and from a sincere intention, they will be imperfect.

order.why: Read the intellect in service to the heart.
Consider reason’s relationship to equity, mercy and solidarity.
shortened: Intellect judges according to justice, nature according to force. Intellect judges according to equity, nature according to aggression. Intellect judges according to solidarity, mercy and love. Nature, on the contrary, is governed by the law of the survival of the fittest, whereas the distinction of man is to be sanctified above such a law.

order.why: Affirm intellectual discovery within the spiritual account.
shortened: The power of the Holy Spirit, enlightening man's intelligence, has enabled him to discover means of bending many natural laws to his will.

order.why: Keep scientific knowledge among the powers described.
shortened: Likewise the Holy Spirit is the very cause of the life of man; without the Holy Spirit he would have no intellect, he would be unable to acquire his scientific knowledge by which his great influence over the rest of creation is gained.
